prompt.context: A retired Fuqua professor is thinking about buying a piece of land in the surrounding Durham area. The land includes 10 acres which is ready for development. The financial goal of this professor is to achieve $20,000 of profit within two years, exclusive of the purchase price.
prompt.question: Is this a good idea? What would you recommend the professor do with the land, and can the $20,000 profit goal be achieved within two years?

clarifying_info.q: What is the land currently used for, or what could it be used for?
clarifying_info.a: First ask the candidate to brainstorm options, then specify agricultural development.
The professor has an educational background in agro-engineering and has consulted on behalf of commercial partners.

clarifying_info.q: How many plants can fit on an acre?
clarifying_info.a: 10 pine trees per acre, 25 rose bushes per acre, 75 beets per acre, 50 saffron per acre.

clarifying_info.q: What is the market growth rate?
Can the professor capture the remaining market share beyond the penetration rate?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, if asked, the client can capture the remaining share of the market.

exhibits.title: Annual analysis of North Carolina market
exhibits.shows: A table comparing four crop types across four metrics: price per plant, cost per plant, market demand (units), and competition control percentage.

notes: Note 1: Assume Y1 start-up costs of $1,500
Note 2: Assume annual maintenance costs of $1,050

framework: Revenue Generation: evaluate farming (land viability, crop type, short turnover for profit) vs. commercial real estate development (investor appetite, community enhancement, longer timeline) vs. residential real estate development (housing market trends, Durham population/growth projections)
Costs: government fees and zoning restrictions, property taxes and professor's tax rate, planning costs (project planning, contracting), alternate acquisition methods
External Factors: major companies moving into the Triangle area, climate change effects on farming patterns, community perceptions and consequences of development
Risks: financing risk, real estate market crash risk, commodity price volatility
Market / Benchmarking: location analysis, similar crops and competition, product demand by specific crop, pricing levers, supply chain considerations, distribution channels (grocers, farmers markets)
Professor-specific: past experience and capabilities, financial health, opportunity cost (different land, different investment vehicle)

questions.prompt: Brainstorm: What are the possible uses for the 10 acres of land?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure brainstorm into at least two buckets. Strong answer covers: Commercial uses (housing/real estate development, commercial real estate), Farming uses (crops, animals). Candidate should remain structured and not list ideas randomly.

questions.prompt: Given the client wants to pursue agricultural development, build a framework for evaluating this opportunity.
questions.guidance: Framework should cover revenue generation (crop selection, demand, pricing, supply chain), costs (start-up, maintenance, government/zoning fees), external factors (competition, climate, community), and risks (financing, commodity volatility, natural disasters). Personalizing to agriculture after the clarifying question is a positive signal.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, determine which crops to grow and calculate the total profit over two years.
questions.guidance: Strong candidate proactively asks how many plants fit per acre. Candidate should (1) calculate penetration-adjusted demand, (2) calculate profit per unit, (3) calculate profit per acre, (4) prioritize crops by profitability per acre, (5) allocate 10 acres optimally, (6) subtract start-up and maintenance costs, (7) sum Year 1 and Year 2 profit.

math.setup: Penetration rate = 100% - Competition Control%. Demand available = Market Demand x (1 - Competition Control%). Profit per unit = Price - Cost. Profit per acre = Plants per acre x Profit per unit. Allocate acres to highest profit-per-acre crops first given demand constraint. Y1 profit = gross revenue - $1,500 start-up - $1,050 maintenance. Y2 profit = gross revenue - $1,050 maintenance. Growth rate = 0%.
steps: Penetration rates: Pine Trees 40%, Rose Bush 80%, Beets 15%, Saffron 10%
Demand available: Pine Trees 5,000x40%=2,000; Rose Bush 1,000x80%=800; Beets 1,000x15%=150; Saffron 2,500x10%=250
Profit per unit: Pine Trees $150-$90=$60; Rose Bush $105-$75=$30; Beets $45-$33=$12; Saffron $75-$51=$24
Profit per acre: Pine Trees 10x$60=$600; Rose Bush 25x$30=$750; Beets 75x$12=$900; Saffron 50x$24=$1,200
Prioritize by profit/acre: Saffron ($1,200) > Beets ($900) > Rose Bush ($750) > Pine Trees ($600)
Acres for Saffron: 250 units / 50 per acre = 5 acres; Revenue = 5x$1,200 = $6,000
Acres for Beets: 150 units / 75 per acre = 2 acres; Revenue = 2x$900 = $1,800
Remaining acres for Rose Bush: 3 acres; Revenue = 3x$750 = $2,250
math.answer: Total profit over two years = $16,500, which is $3,500 short of the $20,000 goal.

questions.prompt: (Optional / harder) What additional levers could the professor use to close the $3,500 gap and reach the $20,000 goal?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm levers across: Pricing (cost-based, value-based, market pricing, segmentation — though commodities limit pricing power), Volume (new markets, up-sell/cross-sell, grow more, bundle), Other revenue streams (farm tours, renting additional land, lowering costs via student labor or lower channel costs).

brainstorming.prompt: What are the potential uses for 10 acres of undeveloped land near Durham, NC?

recommendation: Do NOT recommend the professor buy the land under the current plan: the optimal crop mix generates $16,500 over two years, $3,500 short of the $20,000 goal.

If the professor still wants to invest, they must identify and execute additional levers (pricing optimization, additional revenue streams such as farm tours or land rental, capturing more market share) to close the gap before committing capital.
risks: Demand estimates may be inaccurate — actual penetration could be lower than modeled
Competition could intensify, further reducing achievable market share
Natural disasters, pests, or disease could reduce crop yields
Commodity price fluctuations could compress margins
Zoning or local ordinances could restrict intended agricultural use
Climate change may affect long-term farming viability in the region
next_steps: Validate demand estimates and competition data with local agricultural extension office or market research
Quantify additional revenue levers (farm tours, rental income, pricing uplift) to determine whether the $3,500 gap can realistically be closed
Conduct a feasibility study on zoning, permits, and start-up costs before any purchase
Model a realistic growth rate for demand rather than assuming flat growth
Evaluate opportunity cost: could the same capital generate better returns in a different investment?
